newsitem.title: USA: Okinawa asks U.S. to give back more land.
newsitem.headline: Okinawa asks U.S. to give back more land.

text.p: The governor of Okinawa, where Japanese islanders strenuously object to a continued large-scale U.S. military presence, asked the Pentagon on Thursday to give back more land, including a critical port.

In talks with top Pentagon officials, Governor Masahide Ota said people on the island were "terribly unhappy" about a law approved on Thursday that gives Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto authority to override opposition to extending contracts for private land leased for U.S. military bases on Okinawa.
"People are terribly unhappy about the passage of the law," he told reporters who were invited to sit in on the meeting, a practice used by Ota but very unusual at the Pentagon.
"I'm kind of worrying about that," Ota said, pointing out that 3,000 of 32,000 landowners are opposed to leasing land for the bases, home to 28,000 of the 100,000 U.S. troops based in east Asia.

The Japanese and U.S. government have for decades been overcoming opposition to the heavy U.S. military presence on Okinawa. The opposition reached a fever pitch after the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen in September, 1995.

Ota told the Pentagon's top Asian specialist, Kurt Campbell, that "the people are not satisfied and they want more reductions" in U.S. military operations on the island, 650 miles (1,046 km) southeast of Tokyo.
He proposed that the U.S. give up its extensive military port at Naha and move it to White Beach elsewhere on the island.

Campbell was non-committal, saying the idea would be considered if there was "a suitable replacement" and argued that the U.S. military has already taken a number of steps to make its troops' presence less intrusive, closing some bases, ending artillery drills and changing flight patterns.

Okinawa, in the East China Sea, is home to about half of the 40,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan. It hosts the large Kadena U.S. Air Force base as well as the only U.S. Marine Corps unit stationed outside the United States.

With two aides holding up a coloured map of Okinawa, Ota pointed out that the U.S. military uses 20 percent of the land, 29 percent of the coast and 40 percent of the airspace and pressed for more give-backs by the U.S. side.

When Campbell was explaining how some operations were being moved to mainland Japan and the United States had agreed to shut down the noisy Futenma Marine Corps Air Station within seven years, Ota stopped him, saying "I don't want to argue with you, but I want to explain the facts."

He said that since the end of the Second World War, the United States has returned 60 percent of its bases on mainland Japan, but only 15 percent on Okinawa. "That's why the people are not satisfied," he said.
Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters the United States was pleased the Japanese Diet approved the land lease law.

"We are pleased by that approval," Bacon said. "We believe that the continued presence of U.S. troops in the Asia-Pacific, in Japan and in Okinawa is important. This will allow our troops to continue defending the Asia-Pacific area."
Hashimoto is expected to discuss the issue when he meets President Bill Clinton in the United States next week.
